specimens.format: White-label vinyl first (about 1,000 copies, per Oxide in the Guardian interview); commercial CD single on East West (two parts) per Wikipedia

type.basis: A no. 1 garage hit built on a TV-theme and film sample. Sources file it as 2-step garage; one later reader comment calls it proto-grime. Held as an outgroup: a garage reference point against which grime's characters can be compared.

sound.text: Built around a sample of the BBC Casualty theme plus a spoken skit from the Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels soundtrack; Neutrino voiced it in one take over Oxide's beat (Guardian 'How we made' interview, c. 2019).

Tom Ewing (Popular, 2015) hears a sparse, skeletal beat with deep, hollow bass, time-stretched samples and gunshot effects; the film clip sits where a chorus would be, and the structure feels fragmented rather than built up.
Ewing describes Neutrino's rough, congested delivery as true to pirate-radio MCing: prepared bars, scatting, call-and-response and simply riding the beat (Popular, 2015).
Wikipedia's infobox labels it 2-step garage; many radio stations reportedly refused to play it because of the spoken sample.

context.text: Entered the Official Singles Chart at no. 1 on 6 May 2000 (15 weeks).
Began as a dubplate for a pirate radio show; the pair met at the pirate station Supreme FM and were members of So Solid Crew before signing as a duo (Guardian interview).

Dan Hancox (RBMA Daily, 2019) names it, with 'I Don't Smoke', as the straws that broke the camel's back in the 'garage wars' between the UKG old guard and MC-led crews; Timmi Magic dismissed it as 'kiddie stuff, going backwards'.
In the Guardian retrospective Neutrino says the track 'sounds like the start of what was becoming grime'.

type.basis: Produced by Wiley. Reynolds lists it in his 2005 Grime Primer as garage rap; FACT (2013) calls it vanguard grime. Its string hook and MC-first space anticipate Wiley's later records.

sound.text: Reynolds (Wire 'Grime Primer', 2005, reposted 2015): simple programmed beats and a single violin-flourish hook, with the MCs carrying the track.
Trench (2019): ominous string riffs and harder-hitting drum sequences, like 'a rap cypher in a rave'.
FACT (2013): gritty and gruff, with a skeletal rhythm and bass drone and the MC as the focus.
Mixmag (2018): 'clearly demarcated space for MCs to fill with complex rhymes'.

context.text: A dubplate circulated from late 1999 before the official 2000 release; the crew grew out of shows on the pirate station Rinse FM (Wikipedia).
Reynolds (2005) says it was on dubplate from 1999 and in constant pirate rotation before release; Trench (2019) notes that members Geeneus and Slimzee co-founded Rinse FM.
Crew members included Wiley, Maxwell D, Flowdan, God's Gift, Slimzee, DJ Target, Geeneus, Breeze, Plague, Bubbles and Major Ace; remnants later formed Roll Deep.
Mixmag's Dan Hancox (2018) claims it as the first grime track: a paradigm shift from dark garage to MC-centred tracks.
RBMA (2015): 'Know We' started a buzz for the Pay As U Go and Bow crews, with Wiley selling white labels directly to shops.

sound.text: Steve Goodman (Kode9), writing in Deuce in 2001, calls 'Dilemma' 'ultra-minimal'.
The Quietus (2020): 'Dilemma' is a bare-bones rush of spartan drum hits and a mutating bassline, a moody precursor to minimal grime.
The Quietus (2020): 'Oh No' is sharp-angled, with rumbling bass and MC braggadocio, over a beat sitting between Timbaland-style R&B and UK garage two-step; Lisa Maffia sings the chorus.
FACT (2013) calls 'Dilemma' the 'freakishly minimalist proto-grime flip'.

OCC lists 'Oh No (Sentimental Things)' on its Hip Hop & R&B chart from 16 Dec 2000 (peak 6, 9 weeks); it did not enter the main singles chart.

type.basis: Earliest-dated record in this set that sources widely call the first grime beat (FACT no. 1; SPIN; Wikipedia) and described in an interview as the first 8-bar track released. sound.text: A single 16-bar loop: first 8 bars in a 2-step garage style, second 8 bars stripped to kick and snare; no intro, fade-out ending; a voice sample recurs every 32 bars at the switch.
Stripped down to overdriven bass bleeps and handclaps; lo-fi and minimal with large empty spaces.
Breakbeat garage deconstructed into a minimal, twisted loop.
Producer says he programmed the drum pattern in Propellerhead ReBirth, then sampled a bassline, sequencing in Digital Orchestrator.

context.text: Ranked no. 1 in FACT's 'The 20 best Grime records ever made' (credited Musical Mob, Inspired Sounds, 2002).

Widely considered the first grime beat / a 'year zero'; its minimalism is said to have set the foundations for a more MC-centred genre. Bok Bok named it his favourite example of Youngstar's 'simplistic, brutalist genius' (2014).
Ransom Note interview describes it as 'the first 8 bar track released' and says it sold out within its first week at Blackmarket (record shop); sold heavily on vinyl.
SPIN (Philip Sherburne, 2012) argues it as grime's founding track, noting Wiley's 'Eskimo' as the rival contender later in 2002.

XLR8R (Brion Paul, July 2005) points to Eastern-tinged hip-hop touches, acoustic-guitar R&B smoothness and jungle-style 'precision bass blasts'.
RA (Emeka Okonkwo, 2021) calls Digital Mystikz's 'CR7 Chamber' 'dark and glacial'.

context.text: Rephlex Records discography (Wikipedia mirror) lists CAT 156 'Grime' and CAT 160 'Grime 2' as consecutive various-artist releases.
The Brooklyn Rail says Rephlex 'understandably misidentified' the music as grime, and links the comp to the infancy of what became dubstep.
RA says CR7 Chamber was among the tracks that first hooked audiences, and the duo stayed underground until DJs worldwide noticed in 2006.

Comments under k-punk's April 2004 post on the first Rephlex 'Grime' comp were already disputing whether the FWD/dubstep producers and the MC-led grime scene were the same thing; Hyperdub's steve_hyperdub says Slaughter Mob saw themselves as dubstep.

type.basis: Evidence specimen; its title and a 2020 essay suggest a sample of Cutting Crew's 1986 power ballad, not confirmed by a source.

sound.text: TRENCH (2020) mentions Cutting Crew's '(I Just) Died In Your Arms' as a recognisable sample in Ruff Sqwad's R&G tracks; the title suggests this track uses it, but no source states so. Made on FruityLoops (crew generally).
Afropop pairs it ('Dying in Your Arms') with 'Functions on the Low' as cuts reflecting the crew's 'genuine melodic gifts', borrowing a chipmunked house sample and a cheesy synth tone.

context.text: TRENCH (2020) recalls it on a 2007 Valentine's mix CD from the period when R&G (rhythm and grime) 'had fully arrived'.
